intro: Welcome! Real lectures, talks and podcasts last 20 minutes or more, so in this lesson you practise with extracts from longer talks. You learn to follow the structure with signposts, to hear the speaker's argument and opinion, to recognise British, American and Australian accents, and to take fast, useful notes.
teachingNotes: Recap and build: from b1-listening-main-points the learner knows how to find the main point (who is talking, the topic, the main message; it's often at the start and repeated at the end), the B1 signposts (First/Then/Finally, The main reason is, However, Instead, So, For example) and key-word notes (who, what, when, where, numbers; digits, → and +). Recap that in one line, then go further. A `listen` is at most 300 characters, so 'extended' listening is practised with EXTRACTS of a longer talk: always give the context in the prompt (e.g. 'This is the middle of a 20-minute lecture on urban transport'). Strategies for long talks: predict from the title (what will the speaker probably say?), listen for B2 signposts that show the structure (Firstly / Secondly / Finally, Let me turn to…, Moving on, The key point is…, In other words, To sum up / To conclude), and keep a mental map: which part are we in, and what's next?

Argument and attitude: separate FACTS (numbers, events: '60 percent of the workers…') from the speaker's STANCE (sikap: what they think about the facts). Opinion and attitude words: I'm not convinced (saya tidak yakin), admittedly (memang harus diakui: the speaker accepts a point, but a 'but' is coming), surprisingly (anehnya / di luar dugaan), frankly (terus terang: a strong, honest opinion is coming), I'd argue that, to be honest. Contrast signals: however, that said (meskipun begitu), but, on the other hand. The speaker's real opinion usually comes AFTER the contrast signal: 'Admittedly, X is good. That said, I'm not convinced…' = the speaker is mainly doubtful.

Accents (UK, US, AU): describe the main differences in plain Indonesian as tendencies, not rules (every country has many accents). (1) r after a vowel: Americans say it (car, water, park); most accents in England and in Australia don't (car = 'kaa', park = 'paak'). Indonesians always pronounce r, so British/Australian speech can sound like a word is missing. (2) t between vowels: in American (and often Australian) English it becomes a quick soft d: water → 'wadder', better → 'bedder', city → 'ciddy'. British speakers say a clear t, or (casual London speech) drop it: 'wa'er'. (3) Australian 'ay' (day, mate, late) sounds like 'ai' to others: day → 'die', mate → 'mite'. (4) US 'o' in hot/stop sounds like 'a' ('haht'). (5) can't: UK/AU 'kaant'; US 'kænt' with a weak final t, so listen for stress: I CAN'T go vs I can GO. IMPORTANT: the app's audio uses ONE voice, so never claim the audio shows different accents; accent recognition is taught through this knowledge and real recordings in the resources (English with Lucy's three-accent video).

Note-taking for long talks: key words only (no full sentences), numbers as digits, abbreviations (e.g. = for example, i.e. = that is, approx. or ~ = about, govt = government, w/ = with, w/o = without, b/c = because, vs = versus) and symbols (↑ goes up / increase, ↓ goes down / decrease, → leads to / so, = is / means / the same as, ≠ is not / different, + and / more, ×2 = doubled). Cornell-style notes as an idea: a narrow left column for cues (key words, questions), a wide right column for notes during the talk, and a 1–2 sentence summary at the bottom afterwards. Notes can mix English and Indonesian.

Common errors to target: trying to understand every word and losing the thread of a long talk; taking an example or a detail (a year, a city) as the key point; missing a change of direction after however / that said and reporting the point the speaker only admits (admittedly…) as their opinion; treating a fact as the speaker's opinion (and the other way round); thinking British/Australian speakers 'forgot' the r or that 'wadder' is a different word; hearing Australian 'today' as 'to die'; writing full sentences in notes and missing the next point; fifteen/fifty and thirteen/thirty confusion in numbers.

Limits: listen texts are monologues (no speaker labels), at most 300 characters, A0–B1 grammar only (present/past simple and continuous, present perfect simple and continuous, past perfect, going to/will, modals, first/second conditional, passive present/past simple, defining relative clauses, used to). No third conditional, wish, past modals, participle clauses or non-defining relatives in the listen texts. Answers are short (a key point in a few words, an attitude word, a number): accept the meaning, not exact words. Don't teach phonetics in depth: describe the sounds with everyday spellings.

keyPoints.title: Long talks: listen in parts
keyPoints.explanation: A long talk has a structure. Before you listen, predict from the title: what will the speaker probably say? While you listen, follow the signposts: Firstly / Secondly / Finally (the order), Let me turn to… / Moving on (a new part starts), The key point is… (the main idea is coming), In other words (the same idea again, more simply), To sum up (the summary). Keep a map in your head: which part are we in, and what comes next? Don't try to understand every word.

examples.en: Let me turn to the cost of the project.
examples.id: Sekarang saya beralih ke biaya proyeknya. (bagian baru dimulai)

examples.en: The key point is that people need cheaper housing.
examples.id: Poin kuncinya adalah orang butuh perumahan yang lebih murah.

examples.en: To sum up, the city needs more buses, not more roads.
examples.id: Singkatnya, kota ini butuh lebih banyak bus, bukan lebih banyak jalan.

id.title: Ucapan panjang: dengarkan per bagian
id.explanation: Ucapan yang panjang punya struktur. Sebelum mendengarkan, tebak dari judulnya: kira-kira apa yang akan dikatakan pembicara? Sambil mendengarkan, ikuti signpost-nya (kata penunjuk): Firstly / Secondly / Finally (urutannya), Let me turn to… / Moving on (bagian baru dimulai), The key point is… (ide utama akan datang), In other words (ide yang sama, diulang dengan lebih sederhana), To sum up (ringkasannya). Simpan peta di kepalamu: sekarang di bagian mana, dan apa berikutnya? Jangan berusaha mengerti setiap kata.

keyPoints.title: The argument and the speaker's attitude
keyPoints.explanation: Facts are things you can check (numbers, events). The speaker's attitude is what they think about the facts. Listen for opinion words: I'm not convinced (doubt), frankly (a strong, honest opinion), surprisingly (not what people expected), admittedly (the speaker accepts a point, but a 'but' is coming). After however or that said, the direction changes: the speaker's real opinion usually comes after it.

examples.en: Admittedly, the app is cheap. That said, I'm not convinced it's safe.
examples.id: Memang harus diakui, aplikasinya murah. Meskipun begitu, saya tidak yakin aplikasinya aman.

examples.en: Surprisingly, the older students used the app more.
examples.id: Di luar dugaan, mahasiswa yang lebih tua lebih sering memakai aplikasinya.

examples.en: Frankly, the plan is too expensive.
examples.id: Terus terang, rencana itu terlalu mahal.

id.title: Argumen dan sikap pembicara
id.explanation: Fakta adalah hal yang bisa dicek (angka, kejadian). Sikap (attitude) pembicara adalah apa yang ia pikirkan tentang fakta itu. Dengarkan kata-kata opini: I'm not convinced (saya tidak yakin: ragu), frankly (terus terang: opini yang kuat dan jujur), surprisingly (di luar dugaan), admittedly (memang harus diakui: pembicara menerima satu poin, tapi 'tapi'-nya akan datang). Setelah however atau that said (meskipun begitu), arahnya berubah: opini pembicara yang sebenarnya biasanya datang sesudahnya.

keyPoints.title: UK, US and Australian accents
keyPoints.explanation: These are tendencies, not rules: each country has many accents. r after a vowel: Americans say it (car, water); most English and Australian speakers don't (car = 'kaa'). t between vowels: Americans (and often Australians) say a quick soft d: water = 'wadder', city = 'ciddy'. Australian 'ay' sounds like 'ai': day = 'die', mate = 'mite'. The app's audio uses one voice, so listen to real speakers in the resources.

examples.id: air. US: 'wadder' (r dibaca, t jadi d lembut); UK: 'wo-tuh' (r tidak dibaca)
tempat parkir. UK/AU: 'kaa paak'; US: parking lot, dengan r yang jelas
Semoga harimu menyenangkan, kawan. AU: 'day' terdengar seperti 'die', 'mate' seperti 'mite'

id.title: Aksen Inggris (UK), Amerika (US) dan Australia (AU)
id.explanation: Ini kecenderungan, bukan aturan pasti: setiap negara punya banyak aksen. r setelah vokal (bunyi a, i, u, e, o): orang Amerika membacanya (car, water); kebanyakan orang Inggris dan Australia tidak (car = 'kaa'). t di antara dua vokal: orang Amerika (dan sering juga orang Australia) mengucapkannya seperti d yang cepat dan lembut: water = 'wadder', city = 'ciddy'. Bunyi 'ei' Australia terdengar seperti 'ai': day = 'die', mate = 'mite'. Audio di aplikasi ini hanya memakai satu suara, jadi dengarkan penutur asli di bagian sumber.

keyPoints.title: Notes for long talks
keyPoints.explanation: Write key words only, never full sentences. Use abbreviations (e.g. = for example, approx. or ~ = about, govt = government, b/c = because, w/ = with) and symbols: ↑ goes up, ↓ goes down, → leads to / so, = is / means, ≠ is not / different. Idea: Cornell notes. Divide the page: a narrow left column for key words and questions, a wide right column for notes during the talk, and a short summary at the bottom after the talk.

examples.en: Prices have gone up, so fewer people are buying cars.
examples.id: Harga naik, jadi makin sedikit orang membeli mobil. (Catatan: prices ↑ → car sales ↓)

examples.en: Working from home isn't the same as having a holiday.
examples.id: Bekerja dari rumah tidak sama dengan berlibur. (Catatan: WFH ≠ holiday)

id.title: Mencatat ucapan yang panjang
id.explanation: Tulis kata kunci saja, jangan kalimat lengkap. Pakai singkatan (e.g. = misalnya, approx. atau ~ = kira-kira, govt = pemerintah, b/c = karena, w/ = dengan) dan simbol: ↑ naik, ↓ turun, → menyebabkan / jadi, = adalah / artinya, ≠ bukan / berbeda. Ide: catatan gaya Cornell. Bagi halamannya: kolom kiri yang sempit untuk kata kunci dan pertanyaan, kolom kanan yang lebar untuk catatan selama talk, dan ringkasan pendek di bagian bawah setelah talk selesai.

guidedPractice.prompt: This is the middle of a one-hour lecture on city buses. You hear: 'So that's the history of the city's buses. Moving on, let me turn to the price of tickets.' What is the next part of the lecture about? Answer in a few words.
guidedPractice.hint: Listen after the signpost 'let me turn to'. The history is the part that has just finished.

guidedPractice.prompt: A tech podcast host says: 'The new banking app is fast and easy to use. That said, I'm worried about our personal data.' What worries the speaker? Answer in a few words.
guidedPractice.hint: After 'That said', the direction changes: the speaker's worry comes after it.

guidedPractice.prompt: Your American colleague says she lives in a big 'ciddy' near New York. Which English word does she mean? Write it.
guidedPractice.hint: In American English, a t between two vowel sounds often sounds like a quick, soft d.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write short notes (key words and symbols, not a sentence) for: 'The price of rice has gone up by ten percent, so many families are buying less.'
expected: rice price up 10% so families buy less
rice price ↑ 10 percent → families buy less
harga beras ↑ 10% → keluarga beli lebih sedikit
guidedPractice.hint: What goes up, and by how much? What's the result? Use ↑ for 'goes up' and → for 'so'.

independentPractice.prompt: At the end of a 30-minute podcast about studying, the host says: 'To sum up, the key point is that sleep matters more than extra hours of study.' What is the key point? Answer in a few words.
expected: sleep matters more than extra study
sleep matters more than extra hours of study
sleep is more important than extra study
sleep is more important than studying more
tidur lebih penting daripada belajar tambahan
independentPractice.hint: Listen after 'To sum up, the key point is'.

independentPractice.prompt: You hear: 'Frankly, the new office is too far from the station.' Is this a fact or the speaker's opinion? Answer in one word.
independentPractice.hint: 'Frankly' and 'too far' tell you what the speaker thinks. A fact would be a distance you can check, like 3 km.

independentPractice.prompt: In your notes from a lecture you wrote 'approx. 200 students'. What does 'approx.' mean? Answer in one or two words.
independentPractice.hint: It's the short form of a long word that means 'not exactly'.

assessment.prompt: This is the middle of a 20-minute lecture on urban transport in Jakarta. Listen. What is the key point of this part? Answer in English in a few words.
assessment.listen: So we've looked at the history of the MRT. Let me turn to the main problem today. The key point is this: the trains are fast, but people can't get to the stations easily. Many stations have no safe footpaths, so a lot of people still go by car.
acceptableAnswers: people can't get to the stations easily
people cannot get to the stations easily
people can't get to the stations
people cannot get to the stations
getting to the stations is difficult
getting to the stations is hard
it's hard to get to the stations
it is hard to get to the stations
it's difficult to get to the stations
it is difficult to get to the stations
the stations are hard to reach
assessment.rubric: Correct: people can't get to the stations easily (access to the stations is the problem). The right idea in Indonesian (sulit menuju stasiun) = 70. 'no safe footpaths' alone = 70 (the reason behind the key point, not the point itself). 'the trains are fast' = 0 (admitted first, then 'but'). 'the history of the MRT' = 0 (the part that has just finished). 'people go by car' alone = 30 (a result).

assessment.prompt: This is the start of a 45-minute lecture. Listen to the introduction. What is the last part of the lecture going to be about? Answer in English in a few words.
assessment.listen: Good morning. Today's lecture is about food waste in Indonesian cities, and it has three parts. Firstly, I'll show you how much food we throw away. Then we'll look at the reasons. Finally, and this is the most important part, we'll discuss what families and restaurants can do.
acceptableAnswers: what families and restaurants can do
what families and restaurants can do about it
what families and restaurants can do about food waste
what families and restaurants can do to reduce food waste
what families and restaurants should do
what restaurants and families can do
how families and restaurants can reduce food waste
what to do about food waste
assessment.rubric: Correct: what families and restaurants can do (solutions to food waste). The right idea in Indonesian (apa yang bisa dilakukan keluarga dan restoran / solusinya) = 70. 'the reasons' = 0 (the second part, after 'Then'). 'how much food we throw away' = 0 (the first part, after 'Firstly'). 'food waste' alone = 30 (the topic of the whole lecture, not the last part).

assessment.prompt: This is part of a radio talk about work. Listen. What does the speaker think about a four-day week for every job? Answer in English in a few words.
assessment.listen: A lot of companies are talking about a four-day week. Admittedly, the first results look good: people feel less tired and they take fewer sick days. However, I'm not convinced it can work in every job. Frankly, a hospital can't simply close on Fridays.
acceptableAnswers: it can't work in every job
it cannot work in every job
it won't work in every job
it doesn't work in every job
it does not work in every job
it's not possible in every job
assessment.rubric: Correct: the speaker is not convinced / doubtful that it can work in every job. The right idea in Indonesian (tidak yakin / ragu) = 70. 'it's good' / 'positive' / 'people feel less tired' = 0 (that's what the speaker admits with 'Admittedly'; the real opinion comes after 'However'). 'hospitals close on Fridays' = 0 (the opposite: a hospital can't close).

assessment.prompt: This is part of a talk about a research project. Listen. Which single word shows that the result was not what people expected? Write the word.
assessment.listen: Last year a team gave free bicycles to three hundred office workers in Surabaya for six months. Surprisingly, most of them used the bikes less after the first month. The main reason, they said, was the heat in the afternoon.
assessment.rubric: Correct: surprisingly. 'surprise' = 70 (the right word family). 'the main reason' / 'reason' = 0 (it introduces the reason, not the attitude). 'less' or 'heat' = 0 (facts from the result, not the speaker's attitude).

assessment.prompt: Your new manager from Sydney, Australia, ends a call with words that sound to you like 'I'll send you the report to-die.' Which English word did she really say? Write the word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: today (in many Australian accents, the 'ay' in day sounds like 'ai', so today sounds like 'to-die'). 'to die' / 'die' = 0. 'tonight' / 'Tuesday' = 0.

assessment.prompt: A lecturer from Chicago, USA, tells the class how many students joined the course this year. To you, the number sounds like 'thirdy'. Which number did he say? Write it in digits.
assessment.rubric: Correct: 30 (thirty: in American English a t between vowel sounds often sounds like a soft d, so thirty sounds like 'thirdy'). 13 = 0 (thirteen has a clear t and the stress at the end: thirTEEN). 33 / 3 = 0.

assessment.prompt: This is part of a talk about a survey of young workers in Bandung. Listen and take notes. What percentage of the workers use public transport to get to work? Write the number in digits.
assessment.listen: Let me give you the key numbers from our survey. We asked four hundred young workers in Bandung how they get to work. Fifty percent ride a motorbike, and twenty percent drive a car. Only fifteen percent use public transport, and that number has gone down since last year.
assessment.rubric: Correct: 15 (percent). 50 = 0 (the motorbike riders; fifTEEN has the stress at the end, FIFty at the start). 20 = 0 (car drivers). 400 = 0 (the number of workers in the survey).

blocks.text:
At B1 you learnt to find the **main point**, to follow signposts like *However* and *Instead*, and to take key-word notes. Now the talks are long: a 20-minute lecture, a one-hour podcast, a conference talk. Nobody understands every word of a long talk, not even native speakers. Good listeners do three things:
- **Predict from the title.** A lecture called *Urban transport in Jakarta* will probably talk about traffic, the MRT, buses, costs. Think of 3–4 words you expect to hear. Then you recognise them faster.
- **Follow the structure.** Long talks have parts, and speakers tell you when a part starts and ends with **signposts** (kata penunjuk).
- **Keep a map in your head.** Which part are we in now? What has finished? What comes next? If you get lost, wait for the next signpost and join again.

In this app each recording is short, so we use **extracts** (bagian) of longer talks. The prompt tells you where the extract comes from: the start, the middle or the end of the talk.

id.text:
Di B1 kamu sudah belajar menangkap **poin utama**, mengikuti signpost seperti *However* dan *Instead*, dan mencatat kata kunci. Sekarang talk-nya panjang: kuliah 20 menit, podcast satu jam, presentasi di konferensi. Tidak ada yang mengerti setiap kata dari ucapan yang panjang, bahkan penutur asli pun tidak. Pendengar yang baik melakukan tiga hal:
- **Menebak dari judulnya.** Kuliah berjudul *Urban transport in Jakarta* (transportasi kota di Jakarta) mungkin membahas kemacetan, MRT, bus, biaya. Pikirkan 3–4 kata yang kamu duga akan muncul. Dengan begitu kamu lebih cepat mengenalinya.
- **Mengikuti strukturnya.** Ucapan panjang punya bagian-bagian, dan pembicara memberitahumu kapan satu bagian mulai dan selesai lewat **signpost** (kata penunjuk).
- **Menyimpan peta di kepala.** Sekarang di bagian mana? Bagian apa yang sudah selesai? Apa berikutnya? Kalau kamu tersesat, tunggu signpost berikutnya lalu ikuti lagi.

Di aplikasi ini setiap rekaman pendek, jadi kita memakai **cuplikan** (extract) dari talk yang lebih panjang. Pertanyaannya memberitahumu cuplikan itu dari mana: awal, tengah atau akhir talk.

rows.id: Talk hari ini punya tiga bagian.
rows.note: the start: the speaker gives the map

rows.en: Moving on, let me turn to the results.
rows.id: Lanjut, sekarang saya beralih ke hasilnya.

rows.en: The key point is that people need cheaper housing.
rows.id: Poin kuncinya adalah orang butuh perumahan yang lebih murah.

rows.en: In other words, the plan is too expensive.
rows.id: Dengan kata lain, rencananya terlalu mahal.
rows.note: the same idea again, more simply

id.note: ide yang sama, diulang dengan lebih sederhana

rows.en: To sum up, the city needs more buses, not more roads.
rows.id: Singkatnya, kota ini butuh lebih banyak bus, bukan lebih banyak jalan.
rows.note: the summary: often the main point again

blocks.text: Two traps. First, **examples are not the key point**: after *For instance* or *For example* comes a detail (a city, a year, a story). Second, **the part that has just finished is not the next part**: after *So that's the history… Let me turn to…*, the new topic comes after *turn to*. *In other words* doesn't give new information: it's the same idea in easier words, so it's a second chance to understand.

id.text: Dua jebakan. Pertama, **contoh bukan poin kunci**: setelah *For instance* atau *For example* (misalnya) datang detail (sebuah kota, tahun, cerita). Kedua, **bagian yang baru selesai bukan bagian berikutnya**: setelah *So that's the history… Let me turn to…* (Itulah sejarahnya… Sekarang saya beralih ke…), topik baru datang setelah *turn to*. *In other words* (dengan kata lain) tidak memberi info baru: itu ide yang sama dengan kata yang lebih mudah, jadi itu kesempatan kedua untuk mengerti.

blocks.prompt: A lecturer says: 'So that's how the old system worked. Moving on, let me turn to the new online system and its problems.' What is the next part of the lecture about?
options: The new online system and its problems
Why the lecturer likes the old system
blocks.explain: 'Let me turn to' starts a new part: the new online system and its problems. 'So that's how the old system worked' closes the part that has just finished. Nobody says the lecturer likes the old system.

id.prompt: Seorang dosen berkata: 'So that's how the old system worked. Moving on, let me turn to the new online system and its problems.' Bagian kuliah berikutnya tentang apa?
id.explain: 'Let me turn to' (sekarang saya beralih ke) memulai bagian baru: sistem online yang baru dan masalah-masalahnya. 'So that's how the old system worked' (begitulah cara kerja sistem lama) menutup bagian yang baru selesai. Tidak ada yang bilang dosennya menyukai sistem lama.

material.title: Facts, opinions and the speaker's attitude

blocks.text:
In a talk or a podcast, speakers don't only give **facts** (things you can check: numbers, dates, events). They also give their **attitude** (sikap): what they think about the facts. A good listener separates the two.
- Fact: *Sixty percent of the workers now work from home on Fridays.*
- Attitude: *Frankly, I think that's a mistake.*

Listen for these **opinion words**:
- **I'm not convinced (that) …** = saya tidak yakin … (the speaker doubts it)
- **Frankly, …** / **To be honest, …** = terus terang … (a strong, honest opinion is coming)
- **Surprisingly, …** = di luar dugaan … (the result was not what people expected)
- **Admittedly, …** = memang harus diakui … (the speaker accepts a point, **but** a *but / however / that said* is usually coming)
- **I'd argue that …** = menurut saya … (the speaker's position)

And for **contrast signals**: **however**, **but**, **that said** (meskipun begitu), **on the other hand** (di sisi lain). The speaker's real opinion usually comes **after** them.

id.text:
Dalam talk atau podcast, pembicara tidak hanya memberi **fakta** (hal yang bisa dicek: angka, tanggal, kejadian). Mereka juga menunjukkan **sikap** (attitude) mereka: apa yang mereka pikirkan tentang fakta itu. Pendengar yang baik memisahkan keduanya.
- Fakta: *Sixty percent of the workers now work from home on Fridays.* (Enam puluh persen karyawan sekarang bekerja dari rumah tiap Jumat.)
- Sikap: *Frankly, I think that's a mistake.* (Terus terang, menurut saya itu keputusan yang salah.)

Dengarkan **kata-kata opini** ini:
- **I'm not convinced (that) …** = saya tidak yakin … (pembicara ragu)
- **Frankly, …** / **To be honest, …** = terus terang … (opini yang kuat dan jujur akan datang)
- **Surprisingly, …** = di luar dugaan … (hasilnya tidak seperti yang diharapkan orang)
- **Admittedly, …** = memang harus diakui … (pembicara menerima satu poin, **tapi** biasanya *but / however / that said* akan menyusul)
- **I'd argue that …** = menurut saya … (posisi pembicara)

Dan **tanda kontras**: **however** (namun), **but** (tapi), **that said** (meskipun begitu), **on the other hand** (di sisi lain). Opini pembicara yang sebenarnya biasanya datang **setelah** kata-kata itu.

rows.en: The new bus line carries ten thousand people a day.
rows.id: Jalur bus baru itu mengangkut sepuluh ribu orang per hari.
rows.note: a fact: you can check it

rows.en: Admittedly, the buses are cheap. That said, they're often late.
rows.id: Memang harus diakui, busnya murah. Meskipun begitu, busnya sering terlambat.
rows.note: the speaker's main point comes after 'that said'

id.note: poin utama pembicara datang setelah 'that said'

rows.en: I'm not convinced that more roads will help.
rows.id: Saya tidak yakin jalan tambahan akan membantu.

rows.en: To be honest, the results were disappointing.

id.note: sikap: opini yang kuat dan jujur

blocks.text: Indonesian trap: *admittedly* looks positive, so many learners think the speaker agrees. But *Admittedly, X is good* usually means 'OK, X is good… **but** I have a problem with it'. Wait for *however* or *that said*: the speaker's real opinion is there. Also, *I'm not convinced* is polite English for 'I don't really believe it': it's stronger than Indonesian *kurang yakin* sounds.

id.text: Jebakan untuk orang Indonesia: *admittedly* terdengar positif, jadi banyak pelajar mengira pembicaranya setuju. Padahal *Admittedly, X is good* biasanya berarti 'Oke, X memang bagus… **tapi** saya punya masalah dengannya'. Tunggu *however* atau *that said*: opini sebenarnya ada di sana. Selain itu, *I'm not convinced* adalah cara sopan dalam bahasa Inggris untuk bilang 'saya tidak terlalu percaya': artinya lebih kuat daripada kesan *kurang yakin* dalam bahasa Indonesia.

blocks.prompt: A speaker says: 'Admittedly, online meetings save time. That said, I'm not convinced they're good for new employees.' What is the speaker's main opinion?
options: Online meetings are great for everyone.
Online meetings may not be good for new employees.
Online meetings waste a lot of time.
blocks.explain: 'Admittedly' accepts one good point (they save time). After 'That said' comes the real opinion: the speaker doubts ('I'm not convinced') that they're good for new employees. The speaker says they save time, so 'waste time' is wrong.

id.prompt: Seorang pembicara berkata: 'Admittedly, online meetings save time. That said, I'm not convinced they're good for new employees.' Apa opini utama pembicara?
id.explain: 'Admittedly' menerima satu poin baik (rapat online menghemat waktu). Setelah 'That said' (meskipun begitu) datang opini sebenarnya: pembicara ragu ('I'm not convinced') rapat online bagus untuk karyawan baru. Pembicara bilang rapat online menghemat waktu, jadi 'waste time' (membuang waktu) salah.

blocks.text:
In lectures, podcasts and meetings you hear English from many countries. The three accents you meet most are **British (UK)**, **American (US)** and **Australian (AU)**. Remember: these are **tendencies**, not rules. Every country has many accents (Scotland and Ireland, for example, do say the r).

**1. r after a vowel** (a vowel = the sounds a, i, u, e, o). Americans say it: *car*, *park*, *water*. Most speakers in England and Australia **don't** say it when no vowel follows: *car* = 'kaa', *park* = 'paak', *teacher* = 'tee-chuh'. Indonesians always say the r, so British and Australian speech can sound as if a sound is missing. It isn't: it's the same word.

**2. t between vowels.** Americans (and often Australians) say a quick, soft **d**: *water* → 'wadder', *better* → 'bedder', *city* → 'ciddy'. British speakers usually say a clear t ('wo-tuh'); in casual London speech the t can disappear: 'wa'er'.

**3. The Australian 'ay'.** In words like *day*, *mate*, *say*, the 'ei' sound moves towards 'ai': *day* sounds like 'die', *mate* like 'mite'. Australian statements also often go **up** at the end, so they sound like questions, but they aren't.

**4. American 'o'.** In *hot*, *stop*, *job*, Americans open the mouth more: 'haht', 'stahp'. British speakers round their lips: 'hot'.

**Important:** the audio in this app uses **one voice**, so you can't hear these accents here. Learn the differences here, then listen to real British, American and Australian speakers in the video in the resources.

id.text:
Di kuliah, podcast dan rapat kamu mendengar bahasa Inggris dari banyak negara. Tiga aksen yang paling sering kamu temui adalah **Inggris (UK)**, **Amerika (US)** dan **Australia (AU)**. Ingat: ini **kecenderungan**, bukan aturan pasti. Setiap negara punya banyak aksen (orang Skotlandia dan Irlandia, misalnya, tetap membaca r).

**1. r setelah vokal** (vokal = bunyi a, i, u, e, o). Orang Amerika membacanya: *car*, *park*, *water*. Kebanyakan penutur di Inggris dan Australia **tidak** membacanya kalau tidak ada vokal sesudahnya: *car* = 'kaa', *park* = 'paak', *teacher* = 'tii-cheu'. Orang Indonesia selalu membaca r, jadi ucapan orang Inggris dan Australia bisa terdengar seperti ada bunyi yang hilang. Sebenarnya tidak: itu kata yang sama.

**2. t di antara dua vokal.** Orang Amerika (dan sering juga orang Australia) mengucapkannya seperti **d** yang cepat dan lembut: *water* → 'wadder', *better* → 'bedder', *city* → 'ciddy'. Orang Inggris biasanya mengucapkan t dengan jelas ('wo-teu'); dalam ucapan santai di London, t-nya bisa hilang: 'wa'eu'.

**3. Bunyi 'ei' Australia.** Di kata seperti *day*, *mate*, *say*, bunyi 'ei' bergeser ke arah 'ai': *day* terdengar seperti 'die' (dai), *mate* seperti 'mite' (mait). Kalimat pernyataan orang Australia juga sering **naik** nadanya di akhir, jadi terdengar seperti pertanyaan, padahal bukan.

**4. Bunyi 'o' Amerika.** Di *hot*, *stop*, *job*, orang Amerika membuka mulut lebih lebar: 'haht', 'stahp'. Orang Inggris membulatkan bibirnya: 'hot'.

**Penting:** audio di aplikasi ini hanya memakai **satu suara**, jadi kamu tidak bisa mendengar perbedaan aksen di sini. Pelajari perbedaannya di sini, lalu dengarkan penutur asli Inggris, Amerika dan Australia di video pada bagian sumber.

blocks.text: The *can / can't* trap. British and Australian speakers say *can't* like 'kaant' (a long a), so it's easy to hear. Americans say 'kænt', and the final t is often very weak, so *can* and *can't* can sound almost the same. Listen for the **stress**: *I CAN'T come* (can't is strong and clear) vs *I can COME* (can is short and weak, 'kn', and the stress goes on *come*).

id.text: Jebakan *can / can't*. Orang Inggris dan Australia mengucapkan *can't* seperti 'kaant' (a panjang), jadi mudah didengar. Orang Amerika mengucapkan 'kent' (a seperti di 'ember'), dan t di akhir sering sangat lemah, jadi *can* dan *can't* bisa terdengar hampir sama. Dengarkan **tekanannya**: *I CAN'T come* (can't kuat dan jelas) vs *I can COME* (can pendek dan lemah, 'kn', dan tekanannya di *come*).

blocks.prompt: A podcast host from London says a word that sounds like 'paak'. Which word is it?
blocks.explain: Most speakers in England don't say the r after a vowel, and the 'aa' is long: park = 'paak'. Pack and peck have a short vowel and no r.

id.prompt: Seorang host podcast dari London mengucapkan kata yang terdengar seperti 'paak'. Kata apa itu?
id.explain: Kebanyakan penutur di Inggris tidak membaca r setelah vokal, dan bunyi 'aa'-nya panjang: park (taman) = 'paak'. Pack dan peck bunyinya pendek dan tidak punya r.

blocks.text:
In a long lecture you can't write everything. Good notes are **fast** and **short**:
- **Key words only**, never full sentences. Numbers as digits.
- **Abbreviations** (singkatan): **e.g.** = for example, **i.e.** = that is (yaitu), **approx.** or **~** = about, **govt** = government, **info** = information, **b/c** = because, **w/** = with, **w/o** = without, **vs** = against / compared with.
- **Symbols**: **↑** goes up / increase, **↓** goes down / decrease, **→** leads to / so, **=** is / means / the same as, **≠** is not / different from, **+** and / more, **×2** = doubled (two times more), **?** not sure, **!** important.
- English, Indonesian or a mix: your notes are for you.

**An idea: Cornell notes.** Draw a line down the page:
- **Right column (wide):** your notes during the talk.
- **Left column (narrow):** after the talk, write the key words or questions for each part (*Problem? Causes? Solutions?*).
- **Bottom:** a summary in 1–2 sentences. If you can't write it, you've missed the main point: ask or listen again.

id.text:
Di kuliah yang panjang kamu tidak bisa menulis semuanya. Catatan yang bagus itu **cepat** dan **pendek**:
- **Kata kunci saja**, jangan pernah kalimat lengkap. Angka ditulis sebagai digit.
- **Singkatan**: **e.g.** = misalnya, **i.e.** = yaitu, **approx.** atau **~** = kira-kira, **govt** = pemerintah, **info** = informasi, **b/c** = karena, **w/** = dengan, **w/o** = tanpa, **vs** = melawan / dibandingkan dengan.
- **Simbol**: **↑** naik / bertambah, **↓** turun / berkurang, **→** menyebabkan / jadi, **=** adalah / artinya / sama dengan, **≠** bukan / berbeda dari, **+** dan / lebih, **×2** = dua kali lipat, **?** belum yakin, **!** penting.
- Bahasa Inggris, bahasa Indonesia atau campuran: catatan itu untukmu sendiri.

**Sebuah ide: catatan Cornell.** Tarik garis vertikal di halamanmu:
- **Kolom kanan (lebar):** catatanmu selama talk berlangsung.
- **Kolom kiri (sempit):** setelah talk, tulis kata kunci atau pertanyaan untuk tiap bagian (*Masalahnya? Penyebabnya? Solusinya?*).
- **Bagian bawah:** ringkasan 1–2 kalimat. Kalau kamu tidak bisa menulisnya, berarti kamu melewatkan poin utamanya: tanyakan atau dengarkan lagi.

rows.en: The number of electric motorbikes has doubled since 2022.
rows.id: Jumlah motor listrik sudah naik dua kali lipat sejak 2022.

rows.en: Fewer people are taking the bus because tickets are more expensive.
rows.id: Makin sedikit orang naik bus karena tiketnya lebih mahal.

rows.en: A degree is not the same as real experience.
rows.id: Gelar sarjana tidak sama dengan pengalaman nyata.

blocks.text: Common mistakes: writing full sentences (while you write, the speaker gives the next point); writing every example (write the point, then 'e.g.' and one word); and number traps. fif**TEEN** (15) has the stress at the end, **FIF**ty (50) at the start. The Indonesian *koma* is a point in English: *2.5 million* = 2,5 juta.

id.text: Kesalahan umum: menulis kalimat lengkap (selama kamu menulis, pembicara sudah memberi poin berikutnya); menulis setiap contoh (tulis poinnya, lalu 'e.g.' dan satu kata); dan jebakan angka. fif**TEEN** (15) tekanannya di akhir, **FIF**ty (50) di awal. Koma dalam bahasa Indonesia ditulis titik dalam bahasa Inggris: *2.5 million* = 2,5 juta.

blocks.prompt: You hear: 'Since the new metro opened, traffic in the city centre has gone down, so the air is cleaner.' Which notes are correct?
blocks.explain: Traffic has gone down = traffic ↓, and 'so' (the result) = →: the air is cleaner. ↑ would mean the traffic went up, and nobody says the air is dirtier.

id.prompt: Kamu mendengar: 'Since the new metro opened, traffic in the city centre has gone down, so the air is cleaner.' Catatan mana yang benar?
id.explain: Traffic has gone down (kemacetan berkurang) = traffic ↓, dan 'so' (hasilnya) = →: udaranya lebih bersih. ↑ berarti kemacetannya bertambah, dan tidak ada yang bilang udaranya lebih kotor.

id.intro: Selamat datang! Kuliah, talk dan podcast sungguhan berlangsung 20 menit atau lebih, jadi di pelajaran ini kamu berlatih dengan cuplikan dari ucapan yang lebih panjang. Kamu belajar mengikuti strukturnya lewat signpost, menangkap argumen dan opini pembicara, mengenali aksen Inggris, Amerika dan Australia, dan mencatat dengan cepat dan berguna.
suggestedQuestions: Bagaimana cara mengikuti kuliah kalau aku tidak mengerti setiap kata?
Kenapa orang Inggris tidak membaca r di 'car'?
Bisa tunjukkan cara membuat catatan Cornell?

assessment.lex-1: Ini bagian tengah dari kuliah 20 menit tentang transportasi kota di Jakarta. Dengarkan. Apa poin kunci bagian ini? Jawab dalam bahasa Inggris dengan beberapa kata.
assessment.lex-2: Ini awal dari kuliah 45 menit. Dengarkan pembukaannya. Bagian terakhir kuliah ini akan membahas apa? Jawab dalam bahasa Inggris dengan beberapa kata.
assessment.lex-3: Ini bagian dari talk radio tentang pekerjaan. Dengarkan. Apa pendapat pembicara tentang empat hari kerja seminggu untuk semua jenis pekerjaan? Jawab dalam bahasa Inggris dengan beberapa kata.
assessment.lex-4: Ini bagian dari talk tentang sebuah proyek penelitian. Dengarkan. Satu kata apa yang menunjukkan bahwa hasilnya tidak seperti yang diharapkan orang? Tulis katanya.
assessment.lex-5: Manajer barumu dari Sydney, Australia, menutup telepon dengan kata-kata yang di telingamu terdengar seperti 'I'll send you the report to-die.' Kata bahasa Inggris apa yang sebenarnya ia ucapkan? Tulis katanya.
assessment.lex-6: Seorang dosen dari Chicago, Amerika, memberi tahu kelas berapa mahasiswa yang ikut kursus tahun ini. Di telingamu, angkanya terdengar seperti 'thirdy'. Angka berapa yang ia ucapkan? Tulis dengan digit.
assessment.lex-7: Ini bagian dari talk tentang survei pekerja muda di Bandung. Dengarkan dan buat catatan. Berapa persen pekerja yang naik transportasi umum ke tempat kerja? Tulis angkanya dengan digit.
